extracted.intended_audience: legal NLP researchers, legal scholars, and practitioners interested in applying LLMs for semantic annotation of legal texts
extracted.subtask_description: Assign short legal text snippets (sentences / clause-level spans) to semantic types using a general-purpose LLM in a zero-shot setting, and compare performance to standard baselines and supervised models. The focus is on practical prompt construction, evaluation, and trade-offs (cost, token limits, training-data requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use compact one-sentence semantic type definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The GPT model’s annotations are based on compact one sentence long semantic type definitions provided to the model as a prompt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise definitions for each semantic type (single-sentence) and include them in the prompt template (Figure 2). Note that extremely compact definitions may limit the model's ability to capture nuanced types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Batch prediction prompt template and prompt construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed document type, semantic type names, their definitions, and analyzed text snippets into a batch prompt template that primes the model to generate semantic type predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace template placeholders (e.g., {{document_type}}, {{category_n_name}}, {{category_n_definition}}, {{text_snippet_n}}) and return the list of predicted labels as the completion. Construction should maximize cost-effectiveness but may somewhat limit performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Batch size limited by token budget (4097 tokens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make batches as large as possible to achieve cost effectiveness; batch size is determined by evaluated text snippets that can fit into the prompt (4,097 tokens), leaving space for the completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Batch sizes used: 50 for BVA sentences, 20 for CUAD clauses, 10 for PHASYS provisions. Choose batch size by balancing prompt token usage and desired completion tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: GPT generation settings (temperature, max_tokens, top_p, penalties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set temperature to 0.0, max_tokens to 500, top_p to 1, frequency_penalty to 0, and presence_penalty to 0 for deterministic, factual outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperature 0.0 avoids randomness; higher temperature increases creativity but may reduce factuality. max_tokens controls maximum output length. frequency/presence penalties set to 0 allow necessary repetition (important when outputting labels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metric: micro-F1
rubrics_metrics.description: Report performance of systems using micro-F1 scores (and provide confusion matrices for class-level analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare micro-F1 across datasets (e.g., .73 BVA, .86 CUAD, .54 PHASYS) and use confusion matrices to diagnose systematic errors and class confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline: Jaccard similarity (tokens as sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Jaccard similarity between snippet tokens and type-definition tokens as a simple baseline: assign the label whose definition has greatest token-set similarity with the snippet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline tests exact-word overlap; expect LLM semantic understanding to outperform this when semantics rather than exact wording matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervised ML benchmarking (random forest with grid search)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmark against a traditional supervised statistical model (random forest) evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation at the document level, using grid search for hyperparameter selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grid search space considered n-gram type, number of estimators, and maximum tree depth. Random forest often requires large labeled training sets (often close to 1,000) to match GPT performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervised LLM benchmarking (fine-tuned RoBERTa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine-tune a base RoBERTa model for comparison: fine-tune for 10 epochs, batch size 16, sequence length 512, optimizer Adam with initial learning rate 4e-5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use same cross-validation splits as random forest. RoBERTa requires several hundred training examples to match zero-shot GPT performance on many tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning-curve analysis via varied training set sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Train supervised systems on training sets of varying sizes (20, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1,000, @Max) to determine how many labeled documents are needed to match/exceed GPT-3.5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use random sampling of documents per cross-validation fold; identify the point where supervised models catch up (light-blue/light-green cells in Table 1 indicate parity points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness trade-off in prompt/batch design
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximize batch size to reduce API cost, recognizing that cost-driven prompt compression may limit model performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design prompts and batch sizes with awareness of token limits and desired output quality; cost minimization can reduce available context and thus labeling accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset selection and preprocessing: use manually annotated short snippets
rubrics_metrics.description: Use existing manually annotated datasets that attach expert labels to short pieces of text; filter and process data to produce suitable short snippets for annotation (often sentences or clause-level spans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Datasets used: BVA (rhetorical roles in BVA decisions), CUAD (contract clause types), PHASYS (statutory/regulatory provisions). Some spans may be non-contiguous and referenceable with citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for dataset-specific characteristics (imbalance, definition clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider class imbalance, clarity/quality of semantic-type definitions, and reliance on annotator informal expertise as factors affecting model performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHASYS performance was low due to Response type imbalance (62.4%), less clear type definitions, and nuanced distinctions; these properties can reduce zero-shot effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use confusion matrices to identify problematic classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce confusion matrices (true labels by predicted labels) to analyze systematic misclassifications and classes that are difficult to distinguish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: large number of Evidence sentences misclassified as Reasoning in BVA; Emergency Response labeled as Preparedness in PHASYS; some CUAD clause types are easily confused (Minimum Commitment, Profit Sharing, Volume Restrictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-expert QA and hybrid workflow recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: When low tolerance for annotation errors exists, subject zero-shot LLM predictions to human-expert quality assurance, potentially producing a labeled dataset suitable for fine-tuning domain-adapted LLMs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A human-in-the-loop process can convert LLM outputs into high-quality training data that enables supervised fine-tuning and higher overall accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretability of baseline vs model: semantics vs word-overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that simple baselines (Jaccard) rely on word overlap whereas LLMs leverage broader semantic information, explaining substantial performance differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when judging feasibility of zero-shot annotation: tasks requiring semantic generalization favor LLMs over token-overlap baselines.
